QF.id: SIA Assessment Frameworks Techniques and Standards_20

question.text: When an SIA cannot ethically or practically randomise assignment (e.g., life-saving healthcare for tribal children), which family of methods should be considered next, before falling back to pre-post comparisons?

answer.text: Strict compliance audit of Section 135 CSR spending
Quasi-experimental designs — DiD, regression discontinuity, propensity score matching, synthetic control
SEBI-mandated mandatory disclosures under LODR Regulation 33

explanation.text: The Logic: When randomisation is impractical or unethical, quasi-experimental designs are the next-strongest family of methods in the evaluation evidence hierarchy. Difference-in-Differences (DiD), regression discontinuity, propensity score matching, and synthetic control all attempt to approximate a counterfactual using observational data, providing stronger causal claims than a simple pre-post comparison. The Trap: A strict compliance audit of Section 135 CSR spending tests regulatory compliance, not impact. Anecdotal storytelling has no counterfactual. SEBI LODR Regulation 33 disclosures are mandatory reporting, not a causal-inference technique. Note: The specific family of quasi-experimental methods (DiD, regression discontinuity, propensity score matching, synthetic control) is not listed in the Social Impact Assessors Certification Examination Workbook (January 2026); the workbook discusses sampling, baseline data, data analysis, and regression analysis. The framing above reflects general impact-evaluation methodology.
